facts: Corbridge Roman Town, Corstopitum, was a key supply base just south of Hadrian's Wall.
It is one of the best-preserved Roman garrison towns in Britain, with granaries still visible.
Corbridge itself is one of the oldest continuously occupied places in Northumberland.
Vindolanda is famous for the Vindolanda Tablets, the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
The fort predates Hadrian's Wall itself, with the earliest occupation around 85 AD.
Bardon Mill is the nearest station, with the fort reached by a short bus or taxi ride.
Haltwhistle promotes itself as the official centre of Britain, roughly equidistant from all coasts.
The town sits close to some of the best-preserved sections of Hadrian's Wall.
Haltwhistle is a key stopping point on the scenic Tyne Valley Line.
Hexham Abbey was founded in 674 AD and retains one of the oldest intact Anglo-Saxon crypts in England.
Its Night Stair is thought to be the oldest surviving stairway in England.
Hexham is the main market town of the Tyne Valley.
The Castle Keep, from which Newcastle takes its name, was built in the 12th century by Henry II.
The 'New Castle' replaced an earlier Norman motte-and-bailey fortification.
Newcastle Central station itself is a Grade I listed masterpiece of Victorian railway architecture.
The Tyne Bridge, opened in 1928, became a template for the larger Sydney Harbour Bridge.
It connects Newcastle to Gateshead across the River Tyne.
The bridge is one of the most recognisable symbols of the North East of England.
The Angel of the North, by sculptor Antony Gormley, stands 20 metres tall with a wingspan of 54 metres.
It was erected in 1998 on the site of a former colliery pithead baths.
MetroCentre itself is one of the largest shopping centres in Europe.
George Stephenson, the 'Father of Railways', was born in a cottage at Wylam in 1781.
His birthplace cottage sits directly beside the waggonway that first inspired his interest in engines.
Wylam is on the scenic Tyne Valley Line between Newcastle and Hexham.
Prudhoe Castle is the only Northumberland castle never captured by the Scots, despite several sieges.
It overlooks the River Tyne from a naturally defensible position.
Prudhoe sits on the Tyne Valley Line between Newcastle and Hexham.
Durham Cathedral is regarded as one of the finest examples of Norman architecture in Europe.
It holds the shrine of St Cuthbert and the tomb of the Venerable Bede.
Chester-le-Street is a nearby station, with Durham itself served by other lines.
Lumley Castle, now a hotel, dates from the 14th century and overlooks the Durham cricket ground.
Chester-le-Street takes its name from a Roman fort, Concangis, on the site.
The Riverside cricket ground nearby has hosted international Test matches.
The ruined Whitby Abbey inspired Bram Stoker's Dracula after his visit to the town in 1890.
Captain James Cook served his maritime apprenticeship in Whitby before his voyages of exploration.
Whitby's 199 steps lead from the harbour up to the abbey and St Mary's Church.
The museum is housed in the house where Cook lodged as a young apprentice.
Whitby's harbour was a major centre of whaling and shipbuilding in the 18th century.
Whitby jet, a black gemstone found in local cliffs, was hugely fashionable in Victorian mourning jewellery.
Grosmont is the northern terminus of the North Yorkshire Moors Railway, a heritage steam line.
The line has featured in films and TV including Heartbeat and the Harry Potter series.
Grosmont also connects to the national rail network, linking to Whitby.
Captain James Cook grew up in Great Ayton, though his original birthplace cottage was relocated to Australia in 1934.
A granite obelisk in the village marks the site of the original cottage.
Great Ayton sits at the foot of the North York Moors.
Shildon was a key construction town for the Stockton and Darlington Railway, the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives, opened in 1825.
The Locomotion museum, a National Railway Museum outpost, displays historic locomotives free of charge.
Shildon is sometimes called the 'cradle of the railways'.
North Road station is one of the oldest railway stations in the world, opened in 1842.
The Head of Steam museum here displays Locomotion No. 1, used on the pioneering 1825 Stockton and Darlington Railway.
Darlington was, alongside Stockton, at the very birthplace of the modern railway.
Auckland Castle has been the residence of the Bishops of Durham for over 900 years.
It now houses an important collection of paintings by Spanish master Francisco de Zurbaran.
Bishop Auckland sits on the River Wear in County Durham.
Saltburn's water-balanced cliff lift, opened in 1884, is the oldest of its kind still operating in Britain.
The Victorian resort was purpose-built by industrialist Henry Pease from the 1860s.
Saltburn's pier is the only remaining pleasure pier on the Yorkshire coast.
Redcar was home to one of the UK's largest steelworks until its closure in 2015.
The town has a long sandy beach and a history as a Victorian seaside resort.
Redcar British Steel station, nearby, was named for the works it once served directly.
The Middlesbrough Transporter Bridge, opened in 1911, is the longest surviving transporter bridge in the world.
Middlesbrough grew explosively during the 19th century, dubbed 'the infant Hercules' for its rapid industrial growth.
The town became a major centre of iron and steel production.

landmark: Stockton & the world's first passenger railway
facts: The Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened in 1825, was the world's first railway to carry fare-paying passengers using steam locomotives.
Stockton's high street is one of the widest in England, once used as a market and fairground.
The town sits on the River Tees.
Sunderland has a glassmaking tradition stretching back to the 7th century, among the oldest in England.
The National Glass Centre sits on the banks of the River Wear, celebrating this heritage.
Sunderland was once the largest shipbuilding town in the world.
Poet Lord Byron married Anne Isabella Milbanke at Seaham Hall in 1815.
Seaham developed rapidly as a coal-exporting harbour town in the 19th century.
The town's coastline includes dramatic cliffs and a coastal heritage trail.
The Ashington Group, a collective of miner-artists, became known as the 'Pitmen Painters' from the 1930s.
Ashington produced an unusually high number of professional footballers relative to its size, including Jackie Milburn and the Charlton brothers.
The town grew rapidly around coal mining in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
Alnwick Castle has been used as a filming location for the Harry Potter films, doubling as Hogwarts.
It is the second-largest inhabited castle in England, after Windsor.
Alnmouth is the nearest railway station, with Alnwick reached by bus.
Morpeth's Chantry building houses the Northumbrian pipes, a distinctive bellows-blown bagpipe.
The town is the county town of Northumberland.
Morpeth sits on the River Wansbeck.
The traditional song 'Blaydon Races' celebrates a real horse race meeting held here in the 19th century.
The song remains an unofficial anthem of Tyneside.
Blaydon sits on the south bank of the Tyne, opposite Newcastle.
Maryport was the site of a major Roman fort, Alauna, guarding the Cumbrian coast beyond Hadrian's Wall.
The Senhouse Museum holds one of the largest collections of Roman military altars in Britain.
Maryport was later developed as a planned Georgian port town.
Workington was a major centre of iron and steel production, particularly rail manufacturing.
Mary, Queen of Scots landed at Workington in 1568 after fleeing Scotland.
The town sits at the mouth of the River Derwent on the Cumbrian coast.
Carlisle Cathedral is one of the smallest cathedrals in England, partly demolished during the Civil War for building material.
Carlisle Castle, nearby, has one of the longest sieges in English history behind it.
Carlisle sits close to both Hadrian's Wall and the Scottish border.
The Bedlington Terrier dog breed takes its name from the town, developed by mining communities in the 1800s.
Bedlington was historically a coal mining town in Northumberland.
The town sits on the River Blyth.
HMS Trincomalee, launched in 1817, is the oldest British warship still afloat.
It forms the centrepiece of Hartlepool's National Museum of the Royal Navy.
Hartlepool's headland has a long maritime and fishing history dating back centuries.
The station serves one of the largest teaching hospitals in the North East of England.
It is named after Captain James Cook, born nearby in Marton.
The hospital station opened specifically to serve staff, patients and visitors.
James Cook was born in Marton in 1728, now part of Middlesbrough.
A museum and memorial garden mark the site of his birthplace cottage.
Marton sits just south of Middlesbrough's town centre.
Eaglescliffe sits on the River Tees, close to the historic town of Yarm.
The area developed rapidly as a residential suburb serving Stockton and Darlington.
Eaglescliffe is a key junction station on the line towards Northallerton.
Newton Aycliffe was designated one of Britain's first post-war new towns in 1947.
The site was previously home to a huge munitions factory during the Second World War, nicknamed 'Aycliffe Angels' for its female workforce.
The town was built partly to house workers for new industries in County Durham.
Locomotion No. 1 was assembled near Heighington before its historic first run on the Stockton and Darlington Railway.
Heighington remains one of the oldest railway station sites in the world still in use.
The village retains a traditional green at its centre.
The Stadium of Light stands on the site of the former Wearmouth Colliery.
Sunderland's name reflects its origin as land 'sundered' from the monastery at Monkwearmouth.
The city has a long tradition of shipbuilding and coal mining along the River Wear.
Seaton Delaval Hall is considered one of architect John Vanbrugh's finest works, completed in 1728.
The hall suffered a major fire in 1822 that gutted its central block.
It is now cared for by the National Trust.
Northumberlandia is a huge landform sculpture in the shape of a reclining female figure, formed from surplus quarry material.
At 400 metres long, it is one of the largest human landform sculptures in the world.
Cramlington is a new town developed from the 1960s onward in southeast Northumberland.
Wetheral's red sandstone railway viaduct, completed in 1834, carries the line high above the River Eden.
The village sits within the Eden Valley, close to Carlisle.
Wetheral Priory Gatehouse, a National Trust property, stands nearby.
Kynren is a large-scale outdoor performance telling the story of England, staged near Auckland Castle.
The show involves hundreds of volunteer performers and live animals.
Bishop Auckland has become a growing destination for cultural tourism in recent years.
Whitby's harbour swing bridge divides the town's upper and lower harbours, opening for fishing and pleasure boats.
The town remains a working fishing port alongside its tourist trade.
Whitby's kipper smokehouses continue a centuries-old herring-curing tradition.

landmark: Danby & the Moors National Park Centre
facts: The North York Moors National Park Centre near Danby introduces visitors to the surrounding moorland landscape.
Danby sits in Eskdale, one of the principal valleys of the North York Moors.
The Esk Valley Line, connecting Middlesbrough and Whitby, is considered one of England's most scenic branch lines.
Nearby Goathland doubled as Aidensfield in the long-running TV series Heartbeat.
Goathland station also appeared as Hogsmeade station in the Harry Potter films.
Grosmont connects the heritage North Yorkshire Moors Railway to the national network.

landmark: MIMA, Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art
facts: MIMA opened in 2007 as part of Middlesbrough's efforts to reinvent itself through culture.
The gallery holds significant collections of jewellery and applied art alongside contemporary works.
It sits within Centre Square, part of the town's post-industrial regeneration.
Billingham grew rapidly around ICI's huge chemical works, established in the 1920s.
The town was a planned development built to house the growing industrial workforce.
Billingham sits on the north bank of the River Tees.
Redcar East serves the eastern end of Redcar's long sandy beach, known locally as the Stray.
The town has hosted horse racing on its sands since Victorian times.
Redcar sits on the Yorkshire coast just south of the Tees estuary.
Egton Bridge holds an annual gooseberry show, a centuries-old local tradition.
The village sits in the wooded Esk Valley within the North York Moors.
Egton station lies on the scenic branch line between Middlesbrough and Whitby.
